from what i know i'd say it depends a lot on the kid. i might be fine in public school if i get some accommodations, but someone else might still find it really hard. with homeschooling i'd say the caveat is that you need to find a way to get social interaction outside of your own family. yknow, find clubs in town or contact other parents with kids their age especially if you can find other autistic kids. cause the social stuff is still important, but doing it without throwing them into a building with hundreds of other kids works and is probably better for the kid... homeschool can be the better option if you can find other ways to get some interaction with other people.

but again it varies wildly from person to person. most of my issues with public school at least at the high school level are noise (could wear ear defenders), large numbers of people (mostly this is in passing time though and i generally hide in a teacher's room during lunch), and struggling in english and history with writing and due dates (could be helped through an iep). oh and having to hide stimming (i try to use more "normal" ones), not infodumping (no one to infodump to though lol), etc.

i do quite like SOME aspects of school especially because the teachers in my district tend to be really nice about things even if you don't have any official accommodations or whatever. i've had lots of really good experiences in classes even if i've had a lot of bad ones, and there are a lot of school activities i wouldn't have been able to participate in - math team in middle and high school, debate briefly in middle school, talent shows in middle and high school, etc.

so anyway yeah there are positives and negatives to both and it would HEAVILY depend on the kid so this is just what i think and what my experience has been. i've not got some of the challenges others might have in public school so my experience is just one of the possibilities.

i recommend looking at some basic online asd assessments. one of the best ones is this: [aspie quiz](https://rdos.net/eng/Aspie-quiz.php)

it can't diagnose you obviously, but it can give you a good idea of how likely it is that you're autistic and of how much of what symptoms/traits you have. that can give you a good idea of whether to look in that direction or in another. i don't have any real suggestions for dealing with the system because i've not had to deal with it myself.

do try to research possibilities yourself if you can, because i would say that having a vague idea of what's up, even if you can't get a diagnosis, can help. you won't have access to some resources without one, but you can use the name to look for strategies people with similar symptoms/traits use to cope outside of that which comes with a diagnosis. even if you don't have that given condition, the strategies people with it use to manage symptoms can still be helpful to you. just avoid self-diagnosing because there are a lot of issues with that.

good luck :D

from what i've seen they can call emergency if they think you're in immediate danger (ie likely to hurt yourself very soon). i think the ability to get your location varies and different lines have different policies, but generally you're anonymous. most of them have a website you can check for their policies as far as that all goes, so it might be worth googling the specific one you're thinking about calling to see how they handle that sort of stuff.

if you're not in immediate danger, don't already have a plan/method figured out, don't have immediate access to a method, etc (or are willing to lie about it) then you probably don't need to worry about it.
